title: TB8-29354
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Principal Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the Co-Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and the Minor Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, citizens of Colombia, appeal the decision of the RPD which rejected their claim.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Principal Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the Co-Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and the Minor Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, citizens of Colombia, appeal the decision of the RPD which rejected their claim. The Co-Appellant was appointed the designated representative of the Minor Appellant. The Appellants are submitting new evidence and are requesting an oral hearing. For the reasons which follow, the Appeal is not allowed.
The Appellants fear the FARC.
For questions of fact, mixed fact and law, and law, I will apply the standard of correctness as per Huruglica.1
Accordingly, I will conduct my own analysis of the Record to determine if the RPD erred.

The Appellants have submitted the following documents as new evidence: a) the Google translation of the Spanish word "Camioneta" which translates the word into Van or truck.2; b) an article dated December 11 2018 which discusses the fact that the FARC might be regrouping3.
I will analyse the admissibility of the proposed new evidence pursuant to the test set out in subsection 110(4) and in accordance with the Federal Court of Appeal Decision in Singh.4
I accept that the word "Camioneta" does translate into a van or truck. Therefore I accept the document as new evidence.

The article was published after the RPD rendered its decision and therefore meets the statutory requirement. I note that it indicates that there is information with respect to a "possible' regrouping of the FARC, but it also states that the majority of the FARC fighters have laid down their arms. The article gives no indication as to whether the Appellants would still be at risk if they were to return to Columbia. I therefore give the article no evidentiary weight.
Given the above disposition with respect to the new evidence, the request for a new hearing is denied.

The RPD concluded that the Appellants would not be persecuted if they were to return to Columbia and that there is state protection available to them. The RPD also found that the Appellants had failed to file a refugee claim in the United States. The Appellants raise three issues: a) Did the Board err in its credibility assessment? b) Did the Board err by ignoring and misconstruing evidence? c) Did the Board err in its analysis of Appellant's case due to unreasonable preconceptions about the Appellant's case?5
paragraphs.heading_before: ANALYSIS ON THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: The Appellants allege that the Principal Appellant was assaulted by the FARC on XXXX XXXX, 2014. The RPD did not find this particular allegation credible as it concluded that there was a discrepancy in the Principal Appellant's testimony as to whether he was referring to truck or car. The RPD also had issues with respect to a supporting letter by one of the Principal Appellant's neighbors. I have accepted the new evidence which indicates that the vehicle was in fact a truck and therefore I find that the Principal Appellant was assaulted on the day in question.

He also alleges that in XXXX of 2014 he received a threatening telephone call from the agents of persecution. However, it would take well over a year after the assault in XXXX of 2014 for the Appellants to leave Columbia.

I note that the last contact that the Principal Appellant had with the agents of persecution was in XXXX of 2014, well over four and half years ago and the Appellants have not produced any reliable evidence which would indicate that the FARC is still interested in the Principal Appellant. He testified that he had not had any contact with his family since he had left Columbia in XXXX of 2015. He also stated that if his family would have been threatened by the FARC, they would have notified him. I therefore conclude, based on the testimony of the Principal Appellant, that the Appellants nor their family in Columbia have been threatened by the FARC since the appellants left Columbia. It is reasonable to expect that, if the Principal Appellant was of interest to the FARC, he or his family would have continued to receive threats after they left Columbia. It has been nearly five years since the Principal Appellant was last threatened by the FARC and he has failed to produce any reliable evidence which would indicate that he is a person of interest to the FARC.
I therefore agree with the RPD that the appellants would not be at risk nor would they be threatened by the FARC if they were to return to Columbia.

The RPD also concluded that the Appellants failed to file an asylum claim while living for two and half years in the United States. They were asked by the RPD why they had not filed a claim in the United States and the Principal Appellant replied that they had been advised that it would not be beneficial for them to make such an application. The RPD rejected this explanation. I agree with the RPD in rejecting this explanation.

I note that the Appellants did not challenge this particular finding of the RPD. It is reasonable to expect that they would have provided submissions to indicate whether the RPD had erred with respect to this particular conclusion.

In the Bobic decision,6 the Federal Court has stated that: "... an applicant's reasons for not claiming refugee status in a foreign country must be valid in order to avoid an adverse inference." It is reasonable to expect that someone who allegedly fears returning to her country of residence would make every effort to seek refuge in the first country that she arrives at, especially if that country is a signatory to the Convention. The appellants lived in the United States for two and a half years without seeking such protection.

I find this lack of effort on the part of the Principal Appellant to find out and file a claim for asylum troubling and not demonstrative of the existence of her fear. It is a reasonable expectation that a person with genuine fear of persecution or harm in his country of residence will, absent a good reason, seek refugee protection immediately upon arrival in a safe country.7 The fact that the Appellants did not take this step soon upon their arrival in the United States of America puts into question the genuineness of their fear. From my point of view, the apparent lack of urgency in their actions belies their claim of fear. Furthermore, there was no legal impairment for the Appellant to have made an asylum claim in the United States.8

Professor Hathaway has said that it is appropriate to inquire into the circumstances of any protracted postponement of a refugee claim as a means of evaluating the sincerity of the claimant's need for protection.9

The purpose of initiating a claim for asylum is to seek refuge in a host country. The goal of asylum seekers is not to pick and choose which country best suits their needs before they make a refugee claim. The goal of a refugee claimant is to leave their alleged country of persecution and find refuge in a host country. This goal should be pursued with diligence and haste. The Federal Court stated: "This explanation, in the Court's view, is an unacceptable reason to delay seeking asylum in another country and strongly indicates a lack of subjective fear of persecution."10 In the Garzon decision,11 the Federal Court stated: The Applicant's submission that he did not apply for asylum because it would be granted more easily in Canada or because he would gain permanent residence faster in Canada are not valid reasons for negating the adverse inference that he lacked subjective fear by not applying for asylum in the United States.

The Federal Court has upheld this Board when denying a claim when making a finding of lack of subjective fear based on failure of the claimant to make a refugee claim in a country which is a signatory to the Convention.12 In the Bobic case13 the court stated that an applicant's reasons for not claiming refugee status in a foreign country must be valid in order to avoid adverse inference. In the Cortes case, the court stated: "... this failure to pursue asylum during a period of more than 5 years is markedly inconsistent with a subjective fear of persecution.14 In the Gebetas decision15 the Federal Court stated that even a failure to claim in the United States during a two day stay is sufficient to demonstrate a lack of subjective fear.

In the Garzon decision, the court stated: "A finding that the applicant lacked subjective fear due to his failure to apply for asylum in the United States is sufficient, alone, for the Board to reasonably deny the refugee claim."16
I find that the Appellants' failure to file for asylum in the United States is indicative of a lack of subjective fear.
Given the above conclusions, I see no need to analyze any other issue in this Appeal.
Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of IRPA, the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD that the Appellants are not Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

The Appeal is dismissed. (signed) " Pasquale Fiorino " Pasquale Fiorino January 22, 2019 Date 1 M.C.I. v. Huruglica, Bujar (F.C.A., no.
